What this measures

car-free job access — modeled travel times, 2019 baseline. Each city's headline number is transit_job_access_percapita from the transit4 four-step transportation model: how many jobs an average resident can reach by transit, per capita, under 2019 baseline conditions. This is a MODELED estimate, not a survey or a real-time measurement. This access number appears ONLY on "all"-mode rows — never on a per-mode (bus/tram/subway/rail) row.
Per-mode rows are network coverage, not access

Bus/Tram/Subway/Rail rows describe the NETWORK ITSELF — stops served, route count, route-km, service span, AM-peak frequency (trips/hr and median headway), and an approximate walk-coverage area — computed from each city's static GTFS feed (app/mode_network_stats.py in transit4-server). They are NOT a jobs-reachable or access number for that mode; that would require a per-mode routing run this v1 does not do.
500 m walk-coverage area is an approximation

area_km2 approximates a 500 m walk-radius buffered union of a mode's stop points using a pure-stdlib 100 m grid-count method — NOT an exact circle union or convex hull. See transit4-server/DATA_SOURCES.md and the script's area_km2_grid() docstring for the method. network_km sums each route's longest shape (haversine length) with no de-duplication of overlapping/shared branches, which can slightly over-count route-km on feeds with many branching routes — stated here rather than silently assumed.
The 33 cities (+ Helsinki, network-only)

33 cities across the US, Canada, the UK, and Australia are in the job-access RANKING — every city with a transit4-server run report as of 2026-07-12 (the original 5 committed locally, plus 28 pulled from the production model server the same day, each matched to its 2019 scenario for comparability). Of those 33, nine now carry full per-mode network-coverage rows because a local static GTFS feed was ingested: Boston, Chicago, Seattle, Toronto (2026-07-12) plus New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Portland (2026-07-31, roadmap unit T2). The other 24 cities have NO local GTFS feed — their per-mode network-coverage columns are left blank (never shown as zero); only their job-access ranking numbers appear. Helsinki (also added 2026-07-31) is a 34th city in the `citymode` table ONLY, with full per-mode network-coverage rows but no access-ranking row — it has no four-step access model run yet (that's a separate roadmap unit, T7), so it does not appear in the job-access ranking or the standalone Map tab, only in the per-mode comparison.
Feed coverage caveat

Each city's per-mode counts (including zeros, e.g. Chicago/Seattle/Toronto showing 0 rail routes) reflect ONLY the single agency GTFS feed ingested for that city — a separate commuter-rail or regional operator not present in that feed (e.g. Chicago's Metra, Toronto's GO Transit) is NOT counted here. A zero in a per-mode row means "zero in this feed", not "zero service in this city".
Partial feeds: rail/subway network only (New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles)

Three cities' GTFS feeds cover only ONE rail/subway operator, not the full transit network — their per-mode NETWORK stats (stops/routes/network_km/etc, including the mode=all row) are rail/subway network only, not citywide: New York (MTA subway GTFS — no bus), San Francisco (BART GTFS — no Muni bus/light rail), Los Angeles (LA Metro rail GTFS — tram+subway lines only, no bus). Their JOB-ACCESS numbers (transit_job_access_percapita, jobs_within_45min_transit, transit_pct, score, rank, tier) are unaffected — those come from the separate four-step model run, not from this GTFS feed, and remain fully valid city-wide numbers. Each affected row's Method column states the caveat inline.
How the score works — two scales, on purpose

This app now ships BOTH scales side by side, on two tabs, so you can read whichever is more useful: "Ranking · log" (score_log) and "Ranking · linear" (score_linear). Both are derived from the same underlying number, transit_job_access_percapita, and both keep the SAME city order — a scale only changes how spread-out the numbers look, never who's ahead of whom.

score_log = LOG-scale normalize across the seeded city set: round(100*(ln(x)-ln(min))/(ln(max)-ln(min)),1), scaled 0-100 (lowest city in the set = 0, highest = 100). This is the READABLE comparison: New York and London are ~10x access outliers, and a plain linear scale compresses every other city into the bottom of the range (e.g. Chicago would read 2.8 and look flatly car-needed despite having real transit). The log scale spreads the rest of the field out into honest, comparable numbers — e.g. Chicago reads 37.0 instead of 2.8. Switched to log as the DEFAULT on 2026-07-12; tier (excellent 65+, good 45-64, fair 25-44, car-needed below 25) is always derived from score_log, on BOTH tabs — the tier chip does not change when you switch scales.

score_linear = plain min-max normalize of the same number: round(100*(x-min)/(max-min),1), 0-100. This is the RAW SPREAD — it shows just how far ahead New York (100) and London (~83) truly are over everyone else (Washington ~18.9, Boston ~10.1, Chicago ~2.8, the lowest city 0). Nothing is hidden or smoothed here; it's the unadjusted gap. Added 2026-07-12 alongside score_log so neither view is the only one on offer — log for a readable comparison, linear for the honest magnitude of the gap.

Both scales re-normalize automatically as more cities are appended, so scores (not ranks) will keep shifting as the set grows. Ranking cards default-sort by their tab's score (score_log on the log tab, score_linear on the linear tab), descending; tap a mode button to narrow to just that mode on either tab — the mode filter is shared (same underlying table) so it stays in sync between tabs. The plain `score` column mirrors score_log for any older binding that still reads it.
One feed, two views

The Ranking screen's cards AND its inline map both read the same `citymode` table directly (no embed) — the mode filter buttons reshape both together. The standalone Map tab reads the separate whole-network `cities` table and is unaffected by that filter.
Rank by network metric, not just access score (Frequency / Density / Coverage tabs)

Three tabs added 2026-07-31 (roadmap unit T3) let you rank cities by a per-mode NETWORK metric instead of the job-access score: "Frequency" sorts by median_headway_min ascending (lowest minutes-between-vehicles first — the most frequent service); "Density" sorts by stops_per_km2 descending (most stops packed per square kilometer); "Coverage" sorts by area_km2 descending (largest 500m walk-radius footprint). Each tab reuses the exact same mode filter row and `citymode` table as the Ranking tabs — tap a tab, then tap a mode button (e.g. "Bus") to answer "which city has the densest/most frequent/broadest BUS network?" in two taps. Only the 10 cities with a local GTFS feed (see "The 33 cities" above) have numbers on these tabs; every other seeded city shows blank, never zero, same convention as elsewhere in this app. The New York/San Francisco/Los Angeles partial-feed caveat (previous section) applies here too — their numbers are rail/subway-only, not citywide; each card's Method note states this inline when you expand it, same as the Ranking tabs.
Map: v1 vs upgrade path

v1: mono (single-color) point markers on the citymode map, and tier-shaded markers on the standalone Map tab — the simplest honest options with no boundary data or per-mode marker-color support on hand. Upgrade path: true boundary choropleth once city polygon (GeoJSON) data is sourced per city; per-mode marker color needs a map-node colorColumn engine change (explicitly out of scope for this v1, JSON-only build).
Growing further

All 33 modeled cities from the production server are now in the ranking, with 9 of them (plus Helsinki, network-only) also carrying per-mode GTFS rows. Growing further is a data-ops step, not a rebuild: model a new city in transit4-server (or add its GTFS feed for per-mode network stats), then append rows to `cities` (and, if GTFS is available, `citymode`) from its run report — every screen picks them up automatically. A worldwide catalog of ~1,967 transit feeds across ~68 countries is the long-run intake pool.
